items.title: Taiwan’s chipmaking giant TSMC to invest $1B in Anthropic, OpenAI
items.author: Jeremy Hsu
items.summary: Top chip manufacturer TSMC is ready to invest $1 billion in Anthropic and OpenAI. That would give the Taiwanese chipmaker direct stakes in leading AI developers, even as its own contract chipmaking business has profited enormously from the AI data center buildout. The chipmaker’s board approved plans to invest up to $500 million in OpenAI preferred stock reserved for large investors and another $500 million to purchase Anthropic common shares at the latter’s expected IPO price, according to Reuters . Such an investment may give markets “a shot of confidence as the artificial-intelligence trade shows signs of strain,” The Wall Street Journal reported. But analysts also warned that such circular financing among investors, suppliers, and customers has made it difficult to evaluate real market demand for AI-related hardware and services, according to the Journal. items.title: Review: Apple's M6 iMac is pricey, but it's still a good choice for a clean desk
items.author: Andrew Cunningham
items.summary: The Apple Silicon iMac got its fourth refresh this month. Every other Apple Silicon Mac has found a way to move forward over the last half-decade—we've gotten a more Pro design for the MacBook Pro, a mini-er design for the Mac mini, and a Mac Studio that has finally made Apple admit it doesn't want to make the Mac Pro anymore. But the Apple Silicon iMac has always been more interested in looking backward. It's the thin, screen-on-a-stand iMac design by way of the original Bondi Blue G3 iMac. It's a clean and pretty desktop computer, one I see all the time in small offices and on TV shows that depict small offices. We're long past the days when it was Apple's primary workstation computer. items.title: Big Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.
items.author: Kyle Orland
items.summary: The last few years have seen significant debate over the widespread use of AI-powered tools in game development and the responsible disclosure of that usage to players. That debate has exploded into a full-blown controversy in the indie game development space this week, as Big Walk developer House House has publicly and belatedly disclosed minimal AI use in its popular co-operative puzzle exploration game. This particular controversy has been brewing behind the scenes for months, as judges and jury members for the prestigious Independent Games Festival Awards discussed the issue in private discussion groups. But the debate started to break into public view on Monday when 19 members of the 50-plus-member jury released a signed statement outlining a stance "declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity." Noting "a significant increase in the number of submitted games developer with generative AI tools," the group of jurors called out AI's ecological, economic, psychological, and labor harms in rejecting tools whose use, they said, is still "not a foregone conclusion in our industry." Read full article Comments

items.title: Google pushes privacy angle as Gemini-powered smartglasses debut starting at $395
items.author: Ryan Whitwam
items.summary: Smartglasses have always faced an uphill road to acceptance. Not only is propping a computer up on your nose an uncomfortable proposition, but the privacy aspect has been vexing people since the Google Glass days . Now, Google is ready to take another swing at " intelligent eyewear " for the Gemini era after previewing its plans a couple of times. The first glasses are up for preorder today from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, but they're no impulse buy. These devices are a collaboration between Google, Samsung, and the aforementioned eyewear designers. Gentle Monster and Warby Parker have each designed a few different frames, with options for transparent and tinted lenses. Samsung is providing the computing hardware that fits inside them, and Google has the software covered. Warby Parker has designed three frames for Google eyewear, called Alden, Reid, and Wren (see above). They are available with both standard optical and sun lenses in Pine, Saddle, and Jet Black colors at $395 and higher. Warby Parker is only selling devices in the US. items.title: Anduril says its first satellite can see adversaries maneuver in orbital night
items.author: Stephen Clark
items.summary: Anduril Industries has announced the successful demonstration of a new satellite-based sensor designed to track other spacecraft that may be hiding their maneuvers in Earth's shadow. Funded with Anduril's internal capital, the company's oven-sized satellite launched on a SpaceX rideshare mission in July with a package of tech demo payloads: an edge-compute processor, a power-management system adaptable to different mission types, and a long-wave infrared space sensor capable of detecting other objects in orbit. Anduril reported on the success of the tech demo mission Tuesday. The company's satellite, named Anduril-216, flies about 590 km (366 mi) above Earth, spending about one-third of each orbit in darkness. Anduril-216's night passes allow its infrared imager to shine. Read full article Comments

items.title: NASA's secret weapon in the lunar space race may be ... procurement reform?
items.author: Eric Berger
items.summary: Senior NASA officials held a lengthy news conference last weekend, laying out a series of lunar contract awards, new contract opportunities, and mission decisions. They followed one after the other: landers, nuclear-powered rovers, scouting drones, power generation, storage, and communication satellites. It never seemed to end. "Hopefully, we're keeping industry on their toes trying to catch up to all the solicitations we're doing," said Carlos García-Galán, manager of the Moon Base Program, more than 90 minutes into the news conference. "This is what it takes to do the Moon Base in the timeline we have set forth." Read full article Comments

items.title: T-Mobile illegally imposed 50GB cap on low-income home Internet plan, NY says
items.author: Jon Brodkin
items.summary: T-Mobile violated a New York state law by imposing a 50GB-per-month data cap and reducing speeds to less than a megabit per second on home Internet plans it is required to offer people with low incomes, New York government officials alleged. T-Mobile agreed to a settlement requiring it to scrap the data and speed limits, to offer the required low-income plans to more parts of the state, and to make it easier for customers to find information about the plans. The settlement requires T-Mobile to eliminate the speed limits and expand availability of the plans within 120 days. The alleged legal violation and the settlement are related to T-Mobile's wireless home Internet service, not the company's mobile plans. Governor Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James announced the settlement on Monday, saying that a state investigation found T-Mobile violated the New York Affordable Broadband Act (ABA). Read full article Comments

The request was not limited to journalists involved in a controversial report from a news outlet that Trump said exposed confidential military information in a foreign country. (The outlet is not being named to protect national security secrets.) Instead, the DOJ cast a wide net, requesting extensive LinkedIn data on journalists who had any possible link to the journalists around the time the report was drafted. The majority of journalists have LinkedIn accounts and publish their contact information to encourage sources to connect on the platform, LinkedIn argued. Jones, a managing partner with Square Wave Ventures, joined the board in 1993 when the company was founded. As a veteran who has overseen Nvidia since its earliest days, Jones will serve as a conduit for the institutional memory that departs with Huang. items.title: Jensen Huang’s net worth drops $10 billion as Nvidia stock slides in the fallout of affair scandals with company exec and alleged spy
items.author: Emma Burleigh
items.summary: New details of Jensen Huang’s alleged affairs with a Nvidia executive and suspected Chinese spy have sent Nvidia stock sliding this week. Huang resigned as CEO this morning, and Nvidia’s CFO, Colette Kress, will serve as the interim leader. And now, the billionaire is no longer one of the 10 richest people in the world as his wealth continues to slide down the rankings. The day after the Nvidia cofounder confirmed he had been “unfaithful” to his wife, his wealth dropped by $6.5 billion. His company’s stock fell by as much as 9% by Monday, winding up 4.3% lower at $178.67 per share. And things only got worse when New York Times reporting broke soon thereafter alleging that Huang had a second affair with Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell. The entrepreneur’s net worth now sits at $145 billion, around $9.9 billion lower than his fortune before Sunday’s revelations; Nvidia shared dropped more than 7% in pre-market trading today, adding to a wipeout expected to lower the company’s market cap by $1 trillion in November alone. items.title: 36 direct reports, no heir apparent: How Jensen Huang’s ‘flat’ org may have hampered Nvidia’s succession planning
items.author: Phil Wahba
items.summary: A ‘flat’ organizational structure, in which layers of middle management are stripped away so more employees report closer to the top, has become a sort of Holy Grail in corporate America. Companies from Amazon to Meta to Citi have in recent years slashed layers of management to simplify their reporting structures, foster quicker decision making, and, in some cases, free up cash to fund the AI boom. Few companies had exemplified the flat org more than Nvidia . The chipmaking giant employs more than 30,000 people, and its founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang had often expressed his loathing of bureaucracy. He reportedly had some 36 direct reports and eschewed one-on-one meetings. Employees were encouraged to share suggestions directly with leadership, regardless of how long they’d been with the company or their seniority. This flat structure made Huang—who founded Nvidia in 1993 and helped build and fund the AI boom—central and seemingly indispensable to his company. And it may have contributed to the crisis Nvidia now finds itself in. items.title: Jensen Huang has a ‘rockstar’ reputation in Taiwan. Will it survive now that he’s out of Nvidia?
items.author: Jay Ganglani
items.summary: In Taiwan, Jensen Huang is more than a CEO. The Tainan-born Nvidia founder is a frequent visitor who dines with the island’s tech elite and draws fans wherever he goes. On Thursday, Huang resigned from the top job at Nvidia after reports of two extramarital affairs, one with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly believe is a Chinese intelligence asset. Few places have more riding on Huang’s reputation than Taiwan, where TSMC , Foxconn and other suppliers form the backbone of Nvidia’s business and Huang is treated as a homegrown hero. Analysts there say Taiwanese are likely to forgive his personal failings. The allegations that Chinese intelligence may have exploited his relationships are another matter on an island that sees Beijing’s spying on its tech industry as a long-running national security threat. Huang’s reputation is now in ruins in the U.S. following revelations that he had an extramarital affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese intelligence asset. items.title: Lori Huang, not Jensen, is president of the Huangs’ $9 billion foundation—and co-trustee of the trusts holding most of their Nvidia stake
items.author: Sydney Lake
items.summary: Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia , the company announced Thursday . The move follows two extramarital affairs by Huang, one of them with a suspected Chinese spy and another one reportedly with Kimberly Powell , the company’s vice president of health care, according to The New York Times . Huang admitted in a company memo made public on Nov. 8 to extramarital actions: “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Lori has not commented publicly on the memo. Huang’s position has this week raised questions about Nvidia’s future, including who would take the reins in his absence, given that he’s the face of the $4 trillion chipmaking giant. The board tapped Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO. But in the family’s philanthropy, his wife, Lori Huang, holds the top title. Lori is president of the Jen-Hsun & Lori Huang Foundation , which reported about $9.2 billion in assets at the end of 2024, according to its most recent tax filing reviewed by Fortune. items.title: Andrew Cuomo: Wall Street is ready. Congress needs to catch up
items.author: Andrew M. Cuomo
items.summary: History shows that technological innovations have brought great advances to our nation’s financial system, but only after disruption, opposition and regulatory reform. For over a century, Wall Street ran on paper, phones and people racing across hectic exchange floors. The “Canyon” was ruled by institutional giants whose power extended through the halls of government. In the late 1960s, new technology challenged the status quo, with computers offering electronic pricing and trading. In 1969, a company called Instinet pioneered electronic stock trading. This major disruption threatened the Wall Street establishment and was met with skepticism, hostility and warnings about the perils of electronic systems. But while vested interests were opposed, the broader market was beginning to see the benefits. In 1971, Nasdaq was formed to use an electronic platform to distribute quotes, but most trades were still executed over the telephone through existing brokerage firms. Following the national debacle of the 1987 market crash, when Wall Street was under tremendous public pressure, participation in an electronic execution system became mandatory for market makers. items.title: Why Nvidia turned to ‘strategic’ CFO Colette Kress to clean up Jensen Huang’s mess
items.author: Emma Hinchliffe
items.summary: The saga of Jensen Huang, his reported two affairs, and an alleged Chinese spy has come to, if not an end, at least a pause. Huang resigned this morning as CEO of Nvidia , the chipmaker he cofounded that is at the center of the global AI industry and made him a rock star CEO worth more than $140 billion. Stepping in to stop the bleeding as Nvidia’s share price falls is none other than Colette Kress, the company’s longtime CFO. Kress joined Nvidia in 2013 and has been a key lieutenant at the company, with as much power as any exec might hope to have at a business that was run so completely by one man. (Huang reportedly had as many as 60 direct reports.) Before Nvidia, she held senior finance roles at Cisco and Microsoft . As Nvidia’s stock has soared over the past decade to a market cap that at its height surpassed $5 trillion, Kress has been a key face representing the company to Wall Street. Now, she will become Nvidia’s interim CEO. items.title: Three decision-making styles emerge when people weigh probability words against numbers, researchers report
items.summary: We don't all understand the same words in the same way, and this can affect the choices we make, according to researchers including those from the University of Tokyo. A team sought to compare how people with an autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and people without ASD interpret probability terms. They found that people with and without ASD could be divided into three groups of decision-makers, whose judgment varied depending on the relative influence of positive or negative framing and the numerical probabilities they inferred from verbal expressions.

Targeting the processes that make the body age could have effects far beyond any single disease, potentially easing the burden of several age-related conditions at once.

items.title: Mapping the marmoset's deep-brain cell diversity and building a tool to integrate data across species

By charting over 25 million individual brain cells across humans, macaques and marmosets, a team of neuroscientists, computational biologists and software engineers across 55 institutions, including Princeton, produced a cellular roadmap of the basal ganglia, a deep-seated network of brain regions that aid movement, habit formation and decision-making.

items.summary: A single dose of Moderna's mResvia RSV vaccine was 60.3% protective against documented respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections, 60.2% against RSV-associated emergency department or urgent care encounters and 81.8% against RSV-associated hospitalizations in a population of older U.S. veterans, according to a recent study in JAMA Network Open.

items.title: Researchers play critical role in developing new atlas of brain cells
items.summary: Capturing a complete picture of what causes brain diseases from schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease to addiction has long been a challenge for scientists. But a growing body of evidence indicates that all seem related to the basal ganglia—a group of structures found in the center of the brain that control the body's movements, decision-making processes and habit formation.

items.title: Researchers pioneer new technology to track brain tissue from laboratory to data
items.summary: Scientists studying the human brain have long faced a complex obstacle: because of the scarcity of neurotypical human brain tissue, tissue samples from a single brain must be shared across research entities. Those entities then generate massive amounts of data from their research but often lack a coordinated way to share, combine or reuse the information.

items.title: New analytical method offers potential for faster risk assessment of avian influenza viruses
items.summary: Highly pathogenic avian influenza causes significant damage to the poultry industry worldwide. As the virus evolves, new variants regularly emerge that may differ in how easily they spread and how severely they affect infected birds. Researchers at Wageningen Bioveterinary Research (WBVR, part of Wageningen University & Research) characterized eight avian influenza virus variants in chicken and duck cells. Using mathematical modeling, they identified differences in how these viruses behave in poultry cells. Their paper is published in Microbiology Spectrum.

items.title: Ant colonies defy aging patterns as death risk falls and reproduction rises
items.summary: Getting older usually brings a higher risk of death and declining reproduction. Yet for western harvester ant colonies, the opposite occurs. As a colony gets older, it becomes less likely to die and more likely to reproduce.

items.title: From bush food to biodegradable materials: Unlocking the potential of pigface
items.author: Cecilia Duong
items.summary: An Australian native plant traditionally used by Indigenous communities for food and medicine could help scientists develop stronger, more flexible biodegradable film. UNSW researchers have discovered that adding extracts from pigface, Carpobrotus glaucescens, a hardy coastal succulent, to seaweed-based films can significantly improve their strength and flexibility.

items.title: CCTV is touted as a safety measure for day care centers: But does it work?
items.summary: CCTV has been promoted as one way to make early learning safer in the wake of ongoing reports of child abuse and neglect. It's certainly something families see as enhancing safety in services. But does it help in practice?

items.title: City life leaves subtle genetic traces in Berlin squirrels
items.author: Jan Zwilling
items.summary: Roads, buildings and other infrastructure can restrict the movements of wildlife in cities. As a result, urban wildlife from different areas encounter one another less frequently, potentially resulting in reduced genetic diversity.

items.title: Dark magic mushroom is first to contain both psychedelic and toxic compounds

items.title: Euclid offers best-ever 3D map of the universe to date
items.summary: The Euclid Consortium and the European Space Agency (ESA) have released the first major batch of data from the Euclid space telescope. This release, which captures light from more than a billion objects and covers an area of sky equivalent to 9,500 full moons, lays the foundation for Europe's dark universe detective's largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos. Several German research facilities play crucial roles in the Euclid mission's success.

items.title: Unified framework establishes rules for classifying unconventional magnets

items.title: Lipids from banana peels help cherry tomatoes stay fresh longer
items.summary: Fruits and vegetables keep "breathing" even after they're picked. Respiration consumes sugars and organic acids that contribute to flavor, while moisture loss and continued ripening soften the fruit. These changes shorten shelf life and contribute to food waste. Thin edible coatings can be applied to regulate gas and water transfer and preserve fresh produce. Now, food scientists are exploring whether byproducts we often discard could supply ingredients for these coatings.

items.title: Study finds midlife women face unique need for workplace flexibility
items.summary: New research from the Working for Women Research Partnership (WFWRP) shows overlapping life demands make women ages 40–55 more likely than other groups to both want and need workplace flexibility.

items.title: Noncoding RNAs keep genes on time
items.summary: Building a multicellular organism, even a fruit fly, is kind of like assembling a complicated piece of Ikea furniture. As with furniture, you have to assemble it in the right order. "There are many moving parts, many cell types, many organs, and the sequence and timing of events really matter," says Philippe Batut, assistant professor of genetics and development at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons. "Genes have to be turned on at the right time and the right place, or you're not going to get anywhere."

Through fluorescent imaging, they determined the location of the bacterium, which they named Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola. DNA analysis revealed a minimized genome of just 649,000 bases.

items.title: Sequential peaks in arthropod availability across snow and vegetation help sustain alpine birds
items.summary: The alpine zone is located above the tree line in mountainous regions and is characterized by long winters and short growing seasons. Birds and other animals inhabiting these environments breed during a limited period extending from spring to summer. Arthropods, including insects and spiders, serve as an essential food resource during this time.

items.title: Tiny cracks and a 9-volt battery could help fight deadly superbugs

items.title: More Than Numbers: Portraits of U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents

They are not just numbers. Among them is an elderly car wash owner whom agents repeatedly knocked to the ground as they detained several of his workers. A 6-year-old whose mother says still has nightmares after agents pointed guns at him and his siblings. A high school senior who was detained after she tried to stop officers from questioning her autistic younger brother. A dad who was held for several days and missed his daughter’s third birthday. And many Democrats — fresh off an electoral rout of the GOP — are spoiling for a fight. “I want Pete Hegseth not just impeached, I want him prosecuted. They murdered people in the Caribbean. But just because Congress has a government official dead to rights doesn’t mean that that official won’t evade justice. items.author: Barry Levitt
items.summary: Tony Huge in the docuseries Get Huge —Courtesy of Hulu “A day natty is a day wasted.” That’s the motto of Tony Huge, a prominent figure in the looksmaxxing community. In Huge’s lingo, “natty” means “natural,” as in refraining from using a heavy regimen of supplements popular in the rapidly growing online subculture of men that promotes extreme measures to maximize the potential of one’s physical appearance. Especially popular among young adults and teenagers, looksmaxxing often includes risky behavior like the use of trenbolone, a steroid designed to promote muscle growth in livestock that’s illegal for human use in the United States, and DNP, a toxic fertilizer that can burn fat but brings the potential for deadly side effects. For looksmaxxers, the goal is to achieve peak physical form to become more powerful and attractive to women—life expectancy be damned. Filmmaker Stacey Lee first met Huge in late 2024, when looksmaxxing was still “a very fringe movement.” She was embarking on a project about the phenomenon, which she says has moved “to center stage” between then and the Nov. 10 release of her three-part series Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death , streaming on Hulu and Disney+.

items.title: The Toxic Vengeance of Capital Punishment
items.author: Dominic Erdozain
items.summary: —Max Zolotukhin—Getty Images Two radical ideas have been introduced into human thought, wrote the novelist and humorist Kurt Vonnegut. One was that “energy and matter are pretty much the same sort of stuff.” That was Einstein. The other was that “revenge is a bad idea.” That was Jesus. We are so wired for vengeance, so trained to retaliate, mused Vonnegut, Jesus must be classed among the revolutionaries. Vonnegut was no Christian, preferring to describe himself as a “Christ-worshipping agnostic,” but he dreamed of a world in which the long “chain of death and destruction” is broken. That is why he opposed the death penalty and one of the reasons he despaired of America. items.title: When accessible voting isn’t accessible: A blind voter’s experience at the polls
items.author: Baylee Alger / Wisconsin Watch
items.summary: Reading Time: 2 minutes Shortly before the election I wrote about the barriers to voting I face as someone who is blind. I described how, at almost 27 years old, I had never voted because I worried about a lack of privacy in the process. Traditional ways of voting would require me to get someone else’s help — whether checking boxes on a paper ballot or choosing a candidate on a screen. But while reporting the story, I learned about a machine called the Express Vote, which helps blind and low-vision voters mark ballots electronically, enlarge the print on the screen and use screen readers with headphones. I gave it a try on Election Day. Unfortunately, the machine didn’t work. Here’s what happened and why it matters. Because this was my first time voting, I came prepared, bringing proper documentation. After registering, I asked poll workers for the Express Vote, and they led me over to it. I can only describe it as a large screen, a bit like a giant iPad, set up on a plastic table with a chair in front of it. items.title: Kewaunee County nonprofit offers hope to strays in need
items.author: Baylee Alger / Wisconsin Watch
items.summary: Reading Time: 2 minutes Hope for animals in need is always seemingly in short supply. Shelters are over-full and underfunded, or certain rural areas don’t have easy access to animal shelters or well-funded rescues. A Cause for Paws of Kewaunee County seeks to patch that gap. A Cause for Paws is a nonprofit focused on getting care to animals in need, said Suzie Leist, a founding member. The organization’s volunteers go from township to township in Kewaunee County, establishing and paying for contracts between communities and the Wisconsin Humane Society. “The township doesn’t have to pay for anything,” Leist said. The contracts are important because the humane society is not required to take in animals from municipalities it doesn’t have contracts with, said Rachel Charles, board member with A Cause for Paws. Sign up for Northeast News, our free email newsletter focused on northeast Wisconsin. Since Kewaunee County doesn’t have a humane society of its own, the organization provides an important resource to residents, Leist said. items.title: Can gasoline prices at the pump in Wisconsin be changed more than once a day?
items.author: Tom Kertscher / Wisconsin Watch
items.summary: Reading Time: minute Wisconsin Watch partners with Gigafact to produce Fact Briefs — bite-sized fact checks of trending claims. Read our methodology to learn how we check claims. No. On the retail sale of gasoline in Wisconsin, state law states : “All prices posted shall remain in effect for at least 24 hours after they are posted.” The law is aimed at protecting consumers from deceptive advertising. In 2026, the Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection issued a warning to at least one gas retailer after receiving complaints that prices were raised more than once in 24 hours. Gas prices have been volatile since the start of the Iran war in February. As of Nov. 9, the average price for a gallon of regular gas in Wisconsin was $3.92, according to AAA. A week earlier, the average was $4.23. A year earlier, it was $2.85. The record-high average gas price in Wisconsin hit $4.92 in June 2022, but exceeded $5 in six southeastern counties . This Fact Brief is responsive to conversations such as this one . items.title: Wisconsin Rapids clerk devoted her life to running elections. She died on Election Day.
items.author: Alexander Shur / Votebeat
items.summary: Reading Time: 5 minutes This article was originally published by Votebeat , a nonprofit news organization covering local election administration and voting access. On the evening before Election Day, Wisconsin Rapids City Clerk Jennifer Gossick came home from work and told her husband, Lee, that everything was set for the election. For weeks, she had scrupulously overseen the city’s many election tasks, from recruiting poll workers to managing early voting, accounting for all eventualities. But even as she prepared for Election Day, Gossick was dying of cancer she didn’t know she had. Her failing health was clear to those closest to her: She would tire after taking several steps, having to sit and bend at the waist just to get a clear breath. But Gossick wouldn’t consider — or even discuss — her health until the November election was done, she told her husband. She collapsed the morning of Election Day at her home. She died that afternoon at a local hospital. “She worked every day up until the election to make sure they would run meticulously, and then her body gave out,” Wisconsin Rapids Mayor Matt Zacher said, calling it a “dedication to the integrity of elections in our country.

items.title: Scientists Discovered An ‘Invisible’ Object In Space. It’s Challenging Our Understanding of the Cosmos
items.author: Becky Ferreira
items.summary: Scientists have discovered a bizarre “invisible” object in space that challenges our understanding of stellar evolution and could help resolve longstanding astronomical mysteries, according to a study published on Wednesday in Science Advances . Its orbit and mass are so strange, in fact, that researchers ran thousands of simulations and couldn’t reproduce them. The hidden object is likely an ultra-rare supermassive neutron star, which is the collapsed core that is left over after a massive star goes supernova. Located in a system called J0008+0128,, the object was detected through its gravitational effects on its companion, a red giant star. Massive stars that go supernova either collapse into neutron stars or black holes, both of which belong to a wider family of dead stars known as “stellar remnants.” But for decades, astronomers have puzzled over the so-called “mass gap" between neutron stars and black holes, which is the observed scarcity of remnants between 2.5 and five times as massive as the Sun. items.title: Fed faces tougher inflation fight as pressure builds for more rate hikes
items.author: Courtenay Brown
items.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios Inflation is no longer confined to a handful of trouble spots. Now, Federal Reserve officials are starting to question whether raising interest rates gradually will be enough to contain it. Why it matters: Fed officials had hoped that a relatively modest series of interest rate hikes would be enough to bring inflation under control — more a recalibration than a tightening campaign. But stubbornly high — and increasingly widespread — price pressures are raising the possibility of a more prolonged tightening campaign, with no clear endpoint in sight. That would leave the Fed facing a more difficult balancing act: raising rates enough to contain inflation without unnecessarily damaging the economy. What they're saying: "We have got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing — and we're going to have to deal with that," Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee, who called the inflation data "borderline disturbing," said late Tuesday . Why it matters: Nearly 150 years after Reconstruction, Mississippi sent a Black American to the U.S. Senate for the first time since 1881. The votes pushing Colom toward that milestone came from communities where Black residents spent generations fighting for the ballot. Driving the news: The Associated Press projected the race for Colom on Wednesday, handing Democrats a historic upset over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. By the numbers: An Axios analysis of AP county returns found Colom ahead in 16 of the 18 counties in the Mississippi Delta National Heritage Area . Colom collected roughly 100,000 votes to Hyde-Smith's 62,000 — a 38,000-vote advantage. In 2020, Democrat Mike Espy carried 15 of those counties by about 25,000 votes, according to Mississippi's certified county returns . Colom's share of the two-party vote climbed from about 56% to 62%. items.title: When a Walmart disappears, here’s what happens to nearby stores. It’s not what you’d expect
items.author: The Conversation
items.summary: Shoppers often greet the closure of a Walmart with dismay , while competitors find cause to celebrate. Among critics of the big-box behemoth, a long-held assumption is that once a Walmart disappears , shoppers seeking groceries, household goods, meals and services will flow to businesses down the road. But what if the economic downside of a closure is bigger? We are marketing scholars who have studied dozens of Walmart closures in the United States. We found that nearby stores saw a slump in both monthly shopper traffic and sales revenue by roughly a quarter in contrast to comparable stores near Walmart locations that remained open. Our sample covered 39 Walmart stores that closed across 20 states from 2019 to 2026. This finding suggests a large retailer can play two roles at once. Walmart competes with neighboring businesses for shopper visits and spending. But it can also act as an anchor, giving people a reason to travel to a shopping area in the first place. When that anchor disappears, the loss of shared shopper traffic can outweigh the benefit of having one less competitor. items.title: Can anyone really stop the AI data center boom? What could happen next now that voters have spoken
items.author: Kristin Toussaint
items.summary: On Election Day, Americans made their opinions about the AI data center boom clear. Now it’s up to those newly elected legislators to rein in the country’s high-speed data center development. And there’s a lot they can actually do—particularly on the local level. Data centers were “dealt a resounding blow in the midterm elections,” Mandy DeRoche, director of emerging issues at Earthjustice, said at a press event on November 11. Across 10 states, residents overwhelmingly voted for ballot measures to pause development, require public approval for projects, restrict data center electricity use, and link financial assurances to tax incentives. Congressional and state-level candidates who promised to address AI data center development also won in large numbers. The total number of governors supporting moratoriums will now represent states with 41% of the country’s planned data center developments, according to Cleanview. Huang’s resignation is effective immediately. He is also stepping down from the company’s board. items.title: Democrat Scott Colom wins in Mississippi to become the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction
items.author: Associated Press
items.summary: Democratic nominee Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday in Mississippi’s closely contested U.S. Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction. Colom’s narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations despite having the largest share of Black residents of any U.S. state. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats’ argument that their future runs through the American South. “All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this,” Colom told a crowd of hundreds who gathered at Tougaloo College for his victory party. “I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we can show the country that Mississippi matters.” The Associated Press called the race in Colom’s favor after local officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi. items.title: Congress promised to close the THC loophole. Our kids are still waiting
items.summary: I served as governor of Nebraska from 2015 to 2023. My team delivered for Nebraskans. We cut taxes, made the government work better and defended Nebraska values. I also signed the Nebraska Hemp Farming Act into law. This bill allowed industrial hemp to be grown, harvested, processed and marketed in Nebraska. We took this step to align Nebraska state law with the 2018 Farm Bill . We also wanted to support our agricultural community. This Farm Bill federally redefined hemp. It removed it from the Controlled Substances Act and legally separated hemp from marijuana. This was a well-intended change. Hemp farmers argued their crop was a commodity. They said declassifying it would create new economic opportunities. Congress listened and acted. Our state followed. The results are drastically different from what we anticipated. items.title: Mississippi elects Democrat Scott Colom to Senate in massive upset
items.author: Jason Beeferman
items.summary: Mississippi voted blue, in a shock win for Democrats. Democrat Scott Colom ousted Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state that went for President Donald Trump by 23 points in 2024. He will be the first Black senator elected in Mississippi since the Reconstruction era — and the first Democrat from the state headed to the Senate in 44 years. Colom, a Democratic district attorney, ran a scrappy campaign that saw some national money and resources in the final stretch of the race. Hyde-Smith was appointed to the Senate in 2018 and had since won election to the seat twice, but she faced attacks from Colom that she was out of touch and indifferent to rising grocery and gas prices during Trump’s second term. National Democratic groups hadn't paid much attention to the Mississippi Senate race until an October surge of excitement for Colom drew late spending and attention. Colom's win is a boost to the Democratic Party as it seeks to gain a larger foothold in the South and improve their standing with Black voters. It’s also a major vindication for Colom and other Southern Democrats who argued Mississippi had been neglected for far too long.

Josh Shapiro told reporters last weekend at Crooked Media’s post-election conference. “They're not thinking about whether this is about left or middle or right. They're thinking about how to get problems solved.” “I don't know if the takeaway should be what ideology that people wanted. I think people want results,” Maryland Gov. Wes Moore said at the same event. Democrats’ midterm tidal wave was powered more by voters’ anger at high costs and the Trump administration than by any one ideology. Candidates won tough races by positioning themselves not as progressives or moderates but as anti-Washington populists and pragmatists — some of them even scoring dual endorsements from both the moderate Blue Dog Democrats and progressive Sen. items.title: A Tool Built by Election Deniers Said These Voters Were Dead. We Found Them Alive.
items.author: Doug Bock Clark

Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via Getty Image Ahead of the midterms, conservative election activists discussed plans to wield a powerful new weapon in the war against fraud: a data tool built by one of their own that could identify suspicious voters and help with contesting their ballots. The system was put to the test this week in Forsyth County, Georgia, where a member of the county’s election board provided other officials with what he suggested was evidence of wrongdoing: four allegedly dead voters. But it turns out all four are alive and well, ProPublica determined. The board rejected the attempt to challenge their ballots. The effort, though, shows that even after last week’s blue wave, those who believe the 2020 election was stolen have continued to relentlessly search for ways to contest Republican losses. In Georgia, Democrats swept statewide offices . The board member who initiated the Forsyth County challenge, Max Clavijo, is a member of the Election Integrity Network, a group led by conservative lawyer Cleta Mitchell that works to restrict voting and tighten election laws and rules. items.title: Scientists discover that necks didn't evolve for the reason we thought
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the first animals to venture onto land nearly 380 million years ago had surprisingly stiff necks, overturning a long-standing theory about evolution. Rather than evolving to help animals turn their heads, necks may have emerged as part of the anatomical changes that allowed them to move using their front limbs.

items.title: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe discovers a hidden pattern in the Sun’s chaotic magnetic fields
items.summary: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe has revealed a surprising secret hidden within the chaos of space: turbulent magnetic fields reverse their direction of rotation when examined at extremely small scales. The discovery exposes an unexpected pattern in solar wind turbulence that could help scientists better understand solar activity and predict geomagnetic storms.

items.title: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
items.summary: Researchers have created a quantum computer that stores information in microscopic vibrations, potentially making quantum machines smaller, more powerful, and better at preserving information. The breakthrough successfully demonstrated advanced quantum calculations and could help overcome major barriers to practical quantum computing.

items.title: A massive new simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness
items.summary: A groundbreaking new supercomputer simulation is revealing how the universe escaped its cosmic dark age and transformed into a cosmos filled with stars and galaxies. Called Lumina, it recreates 2 billion years of early cosmic history across a region 1.6 billion light-years wide, capturing extraordinary details that previous simulations could not.

items.title: Earth's fiery birth may have created hundreds of oceans' worth of water
items.summary: Earth's water may have been born in the planet's fiery atmosphere rather than delivered by icy comets or asteroids. Scientists discovered that rocky pebbles reacting with hydrogen under extreme heat can produce water in minutes, potentially generating hundreds of oceans' worth during Earth's formation. The findings suggest that water may be a natural part of how rocky planets form, rather than something that must arrive from space.

items.title: Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong
items.summary: A surprising new study suggests that walking, jogging, and even traditional weight training may be less effective at stimulating bone formation than high-intensity sports involving explosive movements and sudden changes in direction. Researchers found that activities such as football and handball increased markers of bone formation by up to 46%, potentially revealing a better way to protect bones against aging and osteoporosis.

items.title: Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising way that fructose, a sugar commonly found in sweetened foods and drinks, may help aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy release fructose that weakens the bonds holding neighboring tumor cells together, making it easier for cancer to spread. High dietary fructose levels and cholesterol-lowering statins also produced concerning effects in preclinical experiments.

items.title: Common forever chemicals linked to nearly double the rate of aggressive breast cancer
items.summary: An NIH study found that women with high levels of two common “forever chemicals” had up to 93% higher rates of an aggressive form of breast cancer. The discovery raises concerns about the potential health effects of persistent chemicals found in everyday products.

items.title: A new AI model wants to read between the lines
items.author: J.D. Capelouto
items.summary: The Scoop New York-based AI startup millionways on Thursday launched its new AI model that claims to offer insight into human intent and motivations. The company also told Semafor it has raised $6 million in US funding, with investors including football stars Jason Kelce and DK Metcalf. The Thorsten-4 model was born out of a research project in Germany in which dozens of psychologists interviewed more than 7,000 people about their personal lives and aspirations. That data — which the psychologists labeled by hand to capture what people’s words revealed about their motives and thinking — was used to train the model. Millionways cofounders Martin Cordsmeier and Max Weidemann argue that understanding is missing from regular AI models, which are trained on internet text. They see the model as particularly useful in sales and executive hiring, where a search firm could prompt it to evaluate an interview transcript to gauge how a candidate will behave under pressure. “We can add a level of human understanding that the language models cannot get to by themselves,” Weidemann said, adding that the model should be “a decision-making support tool rather than the ultimate decision-maker.” J.D.

items.title: Fallout from Nvidia CEO’s likely ouster could slow Gulf AI buildout
items.author: Kelsey Warner
items.summary: The fallout from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s likely ouster will reach the Gulf, where ambitious AI buildouts depend on advanced US chips. Fear over China’s access to American technology through intermediaries has forced local AI champions like PIF-owned HUMAIN and Abu Dhabi-backed G42 to fight hard for chip access. Huang’s affair with a woman US intelligence officials allege is a Chinese spy will no doubt sharpen that scrutiny. Lawmakers are already pushing for new curbs on chip diversion, a move that could threaten the speed of development here. A friend-of-the-Gulf in Washington is also under pressure as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who greenlit the supply of tens of thousands of advanced GPUs to Saudi Arabia and the UAE, faces allegations that he stalled action against the Singapore firm tied up in the Huang scandal; Commerce denies the account. Still, the region’s relationship with the world’s largest chipmaker has long been one of customer and vendor: Great fortunes are tied to Nvidia, but the loss of the company’s leader shouldn’t undermine its ability to produce silicon. The question for the Gulf is, as it’s always been, about access. Dubai real estate tycoon Hussain Saj

items.title: First Abu Dhabi bank raises 15 billion dirhams for postwar boom
items.author: Matthew Martin
items.summary: First Abu Dhabi Bank, the UAE’s largest lender, will raise 15 billion dirhams ($4.1 billion) through a rights issue to fund its “next phase of growth.” The bank told analysts it sees higher organic growth opportunities rather than acquisitions ahead, positioning itself for a postwar investment boom in the country. Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund Mubadala, which owns a nearly 40% stake in FAB, is backing the deal. It’s the latest bank in the emirate to raise money through an equity sale after Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank raised 6 billion dirhams last year and Abu Dhabi Islamic Bank is raising 1.75 billion dirhams. Banks have been tapping equity more as they seek growth; loans increased faster than new deposits. They have also faced higher provisioning and higher impairments as banks build buffers due to the war. — Matthew Martin

Semafor had earlier reported that Kress, who will address the company’s employees directly for the first time as interim CEO on Nov. 18, was in the lead to run the company on a temporary basis. “The Board has full confidence in Colette to deliver on our commitments to shareholders, customers, partners, and to each of you,” newly appointed board chair Harvey Jones said in a letter to employees sent Thursday, which was seen by Semafor. “The board takes seriously our duty as stewards of this great company.” Jones, the former CEO of chip design company Synopsys, was named Nvidia’s first independent board chair on Thursday. items.title: Nvidia without Huang is like Apple without Jobs: A cash spigot without real innovation
items.author: Reed Albergotti
items.summary: Some Silicon Valley executives are quietly celebrating Jensen Huang’s ouster from Nvidia and the national furor over chip exports to China. The good news for American companies is that tech exports that were going to China are now expected to be redirected to US firms, one person told me. That could accelerate the growth of the big AI labs and other Silicon Valley companies, and hobble Chinese rivals. In the short term, they’re probably right. There’s strong evidence that export controls have successfully slowed China’s technological progress. The problem is that the US can’t win the technological race with China in the long term by slowing its rival down. The bigger and more difficult part of that victory is speeding up American innovation. And that’s where Huang’s ouster is a counter-force to the gains made on China policy. Huang is one of Silicon Valley’s great innovators. In the short term, his ouster won’t be terrible for Nvidia. Nvidia may actually become a more profitable company now, because any new CEO will optimize for profitability, as Apple did under Tim Cook. items.title: The end of the 'Nvidia put' that powers the AI ecosystem
items.author: Liz Hoffman
items.summary: Liz’s view Jensen Huang is out, and with him goes the “Nvidia put” that has underpinned the entire AI ecosystem. Huang, who resigned from his post Thursday, was the AI world’s central bank chairman and human security blanket, always there with a checkbook to backstop, acquire, hire, invest in, or otherwise underwrite the least underwritable corners of AI. That “put” — finance speak for a guaranteed buyer on the other side of a trade — has kept the AI financing and fundraising markets lubricated, even as it invited criticism of their circularity. It’s also helped prop up the stock market and padded 401(k)s for the last couple of years. Nvidia guarantees more than $100 billion of data-center leases , owns $51 billion worth of stock in privately held companies, and another $63 billion in listed ones. Its balance sheet was a sponge that absorbed the market’s growing AI fears and put a floor under deal prices. Whoever replaces him will face much higher stakes, akin to Tim Cook after Steve Jobs at Apple. items.title: UAE billionaires optimistic about foreign investment despite eight months of war
items.author: Mohammed Sergie

They can be forgiven for talking up their own book, but foreign investors seem bullish too. At the Bloomberg Invest Dubai conference on Thursday, Blackstone executives said the firm had deployed more capital in the region over the past year than ever before, and opened a DIFC office for its growing private wealth business. Meanwhile, PIMCO highlighted opportunities to finance infrastructure projects. UAE Investment Minister Mohamed Hassan Alsuwaidi said the country plans to draw more foreign capital into energy, industry, infrastructure, AI, and logistics. He also pointed to shortages of offices and warehouses as opportunities. Real estate has gone through multiple boom-and-bust cycles over the past two decades, but when viewed over the long term, the trend line has clearly been up. Mohamed Alabbar, founder of Emaar Properties — which built the world’s tallest skyscraper — was characteristically upbeat. items.title: US DOJ probes Nvidia as fallout from Huang’s resignation ripples across Washington
items.author: Rohan Goswami
items.summary: Multiple US Justice Department probes threaten to sweep up Nvidia, according to two administration officials, as the fallout from former CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation continues to ripple across Washington. One of those probes, on antitrust grounds, is focused specifically on the chipmaker, these people say, while two other inquiries focus on tech companies Megaspeed and Supermicro. The Megaspeed and Supermicro probes have focused on the involvement of Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy that Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair with before he resigned. There’s no indication that the DOJ would seek to charge Nvidia, or Huang, criminally at this time. Spokespeople for Nvidia and the DOJ didn’t provide a comment to Semafor. Megaspeed and Supermicro didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

items.title: Washington risks misinterpreting Iran's 'peacemaker', according to analyst
items.author: Ed Clowes
items.summary: Washington is at risk of mistaking Mohsen Rezaei’s new prominence for a willingness to make concessions, Iran analyst Alex Vatanka argues. The former Revolutionary Guards commander, now secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, has received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance and is reportedly seen by American intelligence as the figure best placed to deliver a deal across Tehran’s factious institutions. But Rezaei’s comeback owes little to public legitimacy — he lost four presidential bids and his economic ideas were widely mocked — and much to a leadership vacuum left by the war and a network of IRGC loyalists built over decades, Vatanka writes for the Saudi-owned magazine Al Majalla. Rezaei has already shown the limits of his flexibility. He welcomed the letter’s tone, then insisted Washington accept Iran’s conditions first. Yesterday he went further, telling Al Mayadeen that not “ a single speck ” of enriched uranium would leave the country because Iran needs it to build nuclear-powered submarines — a rejection of the core US demand. items.title: STAT+: Scientists debut map of basal ganglia, a key brain region involved in an array of diseases
items.author: Jonathan Wosen
items.summary: A massive scientific collaboration meant to unravel the mysteries of the human brain has produced the most detailed map yet of the basal ganglia, a region closely associated with a wide array of psychiatric and neurologic disorders. Researchers profiled more than 25 million cells, generating a deluge of data that allowed them to generate a “parts list” of what cells are present in the basal ganglia and how they’re arranged. In the process scientists discovered a new type of neuron that appears to play a role in schizophrenia. They also identified cell types linked to depression, bipolar disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Demonstrating the value of the work, the scientists produced preliminary evidence that they can use their more detailed understanding of brain cell types to deliver therapies with increased precision. Authors working in mouse models of Parkinson’s disease showed that a gene therapy designed to work in a subset of basal ganglia cells was as effective as a blanket approach; it was also safer. items.title: AI Is Destroying the Trust Between Writers and Readers
items.author: Illustration by Adam Maida / The Atlantic
items.summary: One evening last fall, a middle-aged couple, heads bent in conversation, approached the table where I sat signing books. “Go ahead,” the woman urged. Speaking softly, her husband explained that he had Parkinson’s disease. Although he hadn’t read my novel The Weight of Ink , it was his understanding that it featured a character with Parkinson’s who chose to die by assisted suicide rather than endure her decline. He had some objections. I was horrified—not because I’d written something that offended him, but because I hadn’t. Helen Watt, the character with Parkinson’s in The Weight of Ink , does not, in fact, end her own life. I didn’t know for certain where his misunderstanding had originated, but I had a guess. Just a few weeks earlier, I’d asked ChatGPT a few questions about my novel; it responded to certain queries with this false rendition of Helen’s plotline. Ever since, I’d worried that the misrepresentation might somehow have a real-life impact. Now, it seemed, it had. Any working writer can expect to be called out for their choices; critique is part of the terrain. items.title: Scott Colom Is Mississippi’s First Black Senator in 150 Years
items.author: USA Today Network / Reuters
items.summary: One fall afternoon in Liberty, Mississippi, in 1961, a white Democratic former congressman and state legislator named E. H. Hurst shot Herbert Lee in the head. Hurst was angry that Lee, who was Black, had been trying to register other Black Mississippians to vote. An all-white jury accepted Hurst’s claim that he had acted in self-defense because Lee came at him with a tire iron. Donald Trump, now the sitting president of the United States, was 15 years old. This was how “negro law” worked in Jim Crow Mississippi, which was essentially a police state. Although many laws were race-neutral in their language, “in a society in which race mattered above all else, ‘negro law’ determined who was punished for what,” the historian Neil McMillen wrote in Dark Journey , his 1989 history of Mississippi. In the 1940s, the NAACP was “virtually forced to operate underground,” because in 1920, the state legislature had made it illegal to “possess or distribute” material that would “disturb relations between the races.” As late as 1961, a white man could shoot a Black man in broad daylight and get away with it. items.title: The Last Trumpist Standing
items.author: Illustration by The Atlantic. Source: Klaudia Radecka / NurPhoto / Getty.
items.summary: Does Donald Trump mean anything? The question could be asked about the president’s promises, which he usually fails to keep, and his podium remarks, which are devoted to free association. But for conservative politicians, policy makers, and intellectuals, the question has a wider bearing. Since 2016, the right has been trying to figure out what Trump means as a political phenomenon. Presidents are transformative when they stand for an idea: Ronald Reagan was personally popular, but what made him historic was the reorientation of American politics toward Reaganism, an assertive brand of small-government, big-stick conservatism. Trump has certainly been transformative, so it stands to reason that there is such a thing as Trumpism. Like pornography, we feel that we know Trumpism when we see it, yet after a decade, it’s still remarkably hard to define. That blurriness has been an opportunity for political entrepreneurs who have tried, one after another, to shape Trumpism in the image of their own ideological beliefs. items.title: Netanyahu’s January 6 Moment
items.author: Erik Marmor / Getty
items.summary: No one can mistake me for a supporter of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, or an apologist on his behalf. Over the years, I’ve published hundreds of articles criticizing him and warning of the great damage he has caused to Israel. My criticism only grew stronger after October 7, 2023, when my entire family was almost murdered under his watch. items.title: Seabirds racing home over the ocean can get jet-lagged
items.author: Jacek Krywko
items.summary: Flying across several time zones often causes jet lag, a feeling when the body insists it's the middle of the night while the clock says it's lunchtime. Now it turns out this nuisance is not exclusive to humans. A new Science study on Manx shearwaters, seabirds that can fly hundreds of kilometers a day over the North Atlantic, shows they jet-lag themselves during their excursions. And because these birds navigate by the Sun, that jet lag leaves a measurable mark—it skews their compass. Clockwork compass Patrick Lewin is a behavioral and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford and lead author of the study. “Manx shearwaters are medium-sized birds, about the same size as a pigeon,” Lewin said. “They are white underneath and black on top, but they have very long wings, and they are closely related to albatross.” Manx shearwaters nest in burrows on coastal islands around the North Atlantic. items.title: The FDA wants to pull its approval of a drug. It’s not so easy.
items.author: Sara Talpos, Undark Magazine
items.summary: In May 2021, the US Food and Drug Administration released a lengthy briefing document on an experimental medication for a rare autoimmune form of vasculitis that often damages the kidneys and lungs. The agency was on the fence about whether to approve the treatment, and it wanted an independent advisory committee to weigh in. Among the questions at hand: Was the drug meaningfully better than existing therapies? Participants in the study, which had been conducted by the California biotechnology company ChemoCentryx, did appear to have slightly higher rates of symptom remission after one year. But according to the FDA, it was hard to interpret the results because the study’s design had been less than optimal. Some advisory committee members expressed a similar view. The effect of the drug, said one, “is just not well verified by this study.” At the same time, many patients, and some physicians, saw in the data a potentially helpful medication, one that might lessen patients’ reliance on steroids, which are highly effective but often cause severe side effects. items.title: Once again, NASA is asking for ideas to rescue Hubble from certain death
items.author: Stephen Clark
items.summary: The Hubble Space Telescope still shines in the eyes of astronomers after 36 years in orbit, but it is not as nimble as it once was. Left alone, the observatory will plunge back into the atmosphere in the early-to-mid-2030s, closing the book on one of the most famous scientific instruments of the century. NASA last raised the orbit of Hubble in 2002, when the Space Shuttle Columbia visited the observatory for a servicing mission. The final shuttle servicing flight in 2009 did not reboost the telescope's orbit, and with the retirement of the shuttle fleet two years later, Hubble has steadily lost altitude with no way to stave off eventual destruction. The space agency released a Request For Information (RFI) on Thursday asking commercial companies for ideas on how to reboost, service, or a controlled disposal of Hubble. Responses are due November 30. Specifically, NASA is looking for information about companies' current and near-term capabilities for capturing Hubble and boosting it to an altitude of at least 373 miles (600 km), enhancing the telescope's performance, or guiding Hubble to a controlled reentry. American workers are taking home less of the country’s overall income, data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics shows, and employment in the U.S. is set to continue to slow. Labor share, or the portion of the U.S.’s economic output that workers receive through salary and wages, decreased to 52.8% in the second quarter of 2026, its lowest level since the BLS started recording this data in 1947, according to its labor productivity and costs report . In the previous quarter, labor share was at 53.6%. This decade, the labor share average was about 55.6%. That’s despite corporate earnings skyrocketing, with profits for Fortune 500 companies hitting a record $2.1 trillion in 2025. The U.S. GDP grew 3.4% in the third quarter last year, exceeding economists’ predictions. That growth has not only come at the expense of how much of the pie of wealth workers are taking home, but also how many Americans are in the workforce, economists warn. “That decline in the share of labor has got to be either falling earnings or falling numbers of people,” Raymond Robertson, a labor economist at Texas A&M

items.title: The EPA is quietly killing its web archive
items.author: Rachel Santarsiero, Mother Jones
items.summary: In a little-noticed webpage update, the Environmental Protection Agency has announced a plan to decommission its online web archive at the end of the year, a move that would wipe tens of thousands of publicly available environmental resources from the web. The discreet banner notice comes in stark contrast to EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin’s recent public takedowns of the agency’s power plant pollution standards and federal methane regulatory system . “The EPA’s online archive makes information about a wide variety of environmental issues and past policies available to the public, dating back at least 20 years,” said Gretchen Gehrke, co-founder of the Environmental Data and Governance Initiative, or EDGI. “This information is irreplaceable, and if the archive is decommissioned, that information will be lost forever.” For decades, the web archive has been an unparalleled resource for researchers, legislators, policymakers, and the public writ large. It houses everything from fact sheets and environmental reports to agency policy changes and regulatory actions, making it a tool for “ democratic oversight ,” according to Gehrke, who for 10 years has been tracking changes to vulnerable f

items.title: Trump cut funding for farmers — then unlocked billions for them before Election Day
items.author: Frida Garza
items.summary: The last two years have been a rough going for farmers and ranchers in the U.S. Rollbacks to several Department of Agriculture programs have cut available funding and left producers in the dark. Last year, farm groups sued the federal agency after it deleted multiple webpages that mentioned climate change, including some with critical information for planning around extreme weather. (Early this year, the ag department agreed to restore the webpages in a settlement.) Just this month, the USDA cut solar from a popular renewable energy grant program and dealt another setback to farmers who wish to lower their utility bills and pad their incomes by installing solar panels on their land. Meanwhile, cattle ranchers in the U.S. have been frustrated by high beef prices. The average price of ground beef has been steadily climbing since the COVID-19 pandemic, reaching new records in the last two years. Persistent droughts contributing to historically low herd sizes have also added to ranchers’ plight. items.title: Acute kidney injury up for older patients, men with OD-involved hospitalization
items.summary: Acute kidney injury (AKI) occurs more often among older patients and men with drug overdose–involved hospitalizations, while severe inpatient courses disproportionately affect younger patients, according to research published in the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.

items.title: Personalized score uses ten blood markers to flag disease risk and assess healthy aging
items.summary: Studies conducted in various countries indicate that approximately 60% of people over age 65 currently live with two or more chronic conditions. With the aim of reversing this trend and promoting healthy aging, European researchers have created a new personalized indicator that provides a detailed snapshot of a patient's metabolism by analyzing, with high precision, the chemicals the body produces to function.

items.title: Reversing radiation-activated immune suppression in cancer
items.summary: Researchers at the University of Chicago have identified a mechanism to make immune cells reprogrammed by radiation therapy attack tumors rather than protect them. The study, published in Cancer Cell, shows that radiation activates a protein called TET2 on immune cells in bone marrow, where it removes chemical tags from RNA and locks these cells into an immune-suppressing state.

items.title: New swab test could spare some women a painful biopsy for endometrial cancer
items.summary: A simple vaginal swab may one day help women with abnormal bleeding learn whether they have endometrial cancer without first going through a painful biopsy.

items.title: Treatment with norrin helps maintain healthy blood vessels and preserve vision in diabetic rats
items.summary: Millions of people in the U.S. are affected by diabetic retinopathy, a complication of diabetes that affects the eyes. The condition is caused by damage to the blood vessels in the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. At first, diabetic retinopathy might not cause any symptoms, or the problems might be mild. However, if the underlying diabetes remains poorly managed, it can lead to blindness.

items.title: Looking for bats after dark can help science—and change how we see them
items.author: Kelly Sheldrick, Rochelle Steven, Trish Fleming
items.summary: What's that chirping sound coming through the detector? Did you feel something whiz past? Those are just some ways people react when they encounter microbats for the first time. Microbats are small, mostly nocturnal mammals that use ultrasonic sounds to navigate and hunt at night. They do this through echolocation, producing calls and listening to the echoes that bounce back from objects and prey.

items.title: Rare fossil discovery reveals new dinosaur species that specialized in eating fruit
items.summary: Among the ravenous carnivores and lumbering herbivores that roamed the Cretaceous landscape, another kind of dinosaur was evolving that started to eat something else: the plants that began to flower and produce fruit. The discovery by paleontologists from Stony Brook University, Royal Ontario Museum (ROM) and the North Dakota Geological Survey reveals that a new species, Infernogallus jamesi—a type of small oviraptorosaur—had chewing muscles for mashing soft food, making it the first known dinosaur that specifically ate fruit.

items.title: Rare Iron Age Celtic helmet discovered in northeastern Poland far from its homeland
items.summary: Around 2,400 years ago, at Łysa Góra in Poland, a group of people took a bronze helmet, crushed it, broke it into pieces and threw it into a pit with iron adzes and a scythe. Such helmets are sometimes found in lavish graves of the Celtic warrior elite, from Champagne, France, to Dürrnberg, Austria.

items.title: Calling species 'invasive'—and culling them—isn't done lightly. But it matters to Australia's threatened species
items.summary: It may sound abstract, but distinctions between "native," "introduced" or "invasive" species can often be life or death. Species considered invasive in Australia—such as European rabbits and feral pigs—are often culled, while most native animals are generally left alone.

For this to happen, however, connections must carry fragile quantum information without destroying it.

items.title: When Electric Cars Were for Women
items.author: Allison Marsh
items.summary: At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000. For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place. Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. items.author: Steven W. Thrasher
items.summary: This story was supported by the Pulitzer Center and the Fund for Investigative Journalism. JOHANNESBURG, SOUTH AFRICA — When it opened in early 2024, Engage Men’s Health Clinic served as a free, one-stop shop for sexual health, gender-affirming medical care, and HIV prevention, testing, and treatment. Located within a short distance of seven universities, it was a place where many college students came before “they’d even had sex for the first time,” a former worker told The Intercept. This made Engage a “high-impact” clinic for distribution of the HIV prevention drug PrEP. The building, on a tree-lined stretch of Reserve Street in Johannesburg, was adorned with the logo for the President’s Plan For AIDS Relief, or PEPFAR; a rainbow-colored mural of Simon Tseko Nkoli, the gay anti-apartheid activist who helped start one of Africa’s first Pride celebrations and who died of AIDS in 1998; and a sign for USAID saying the site was a gift “from the American people.” Today, it would be very hard to get help here, despite the welcoming-but-outdated signage. items.title: Why You Shouldn't Toss Your Old Halloween Pumpkins In The Trash
items.author: Simmone Shah
items.summary: Halloween pumpkin decoration by the Navy Pier in Chicago, United States, on October 19, 2022. —Beata Zawrzel—Getty Images The only thing scarier than Halloween ? Getting rid of a sad looking jack-o’-lantern when it's over. When confronted with a rotting, deflating carved pumpkin, your first instinct might be to beeline to the trash as quickly as possible. But experts caution against doing so—warning that trashing pumpkins, and thus sending them to landfill, can release harmful greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. “Everybody throws them out from Halloween to right after Thanksgiving,” says Kay McKeen, executive director at Scarce, an environmental education non-profit. “It's a huge burst of methane gas that's going into the landfill all at one time.” Why shouldn’t you trash your pumpkin? When pumpkins are sent to landfill, they release methane, a potent greenhouse gas that, over a 20 year period, is around 80 times more powerful at trapping heat in the atmosphere when compared to carbon dioxide. items.summary: The site of U.S. President Donald Trump's planned triumphal arch is seen from the top of the Washington Monument in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 22, 2026. —Saul Loeb—AFP via Getty Images Washington, D.C., and Virginia sued the National Park Service and Interior Department on Saturday in a last-minute bid to stop construction on President Donald Trump’s proposed 250-foot triumphal arch . The Trump Administration has said that construction could begin as early as next week. The new challenge joins two existing lawsuits against the arch, adding to a series of legal battles testing the limits of Trump’s authority to remake Washington. Calling the project “flagrantly unlawful,” the lawsuit points to the Commemorative Works Act , which requires Congressional authorization for memorials on federal land in Washington and its environs. The lawsuit also alleges violations of the Administrative Procedure Act, the National Environmental Policy Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act, arguing that the Administration failed to adequately assess the project’s effects and consult as required. items.author: Stephanie Zacharek
items.summary: Nicholas Galitzine as John McLaughry in The Mosquito Bowl —Courtesy of Netflix When you’re a kid, young men going off to war look like men. When you’re a grown-up, you see that they’re really just boys. If The Mosquito Bowl gets close to any essential truth, it’s that one. This is director Peter Berg’s retelling of a true story involving young football stars who went off to fight in the Pacific during World War II, focusing on four real-life figures: Dave Schreiner and Bob Bauman (played by Tom Francis and Bill Skarsgård ) were teammates and close friends playing for the University of Wisconsin; Tony Butkovich (Ray Nicholson, son of Jack) was a fullback for Purdue; and John McLaughry ( Nicholas Galitzine ) had graduated from Brown University and been drafted into the NFL by the time the war had started. items.title: New Census data reveal a homeowner-renter divide in America's electric-car transition
items.author: Russell Contreras
items.summary: Data: U.S. Census Bureau, 2025 American Community Survey 1-year estimates; Table: Russell Contreras/Axios Homeowners were nearly twice as likely as renters to have an electric vehicle in 2025, new Census data show, revealing a striking divide in America's shift to electric cars. Why it matters : Homeownership is just one factor in EV adoption, but reliable access to charging is critical — giving homeowners with private driveways or garages an advantage over renters, particularly those in multifamily buildings. By the numbers: About 7.3 million U.S. households — 5.5% of the nation's 134 million — reported having at least one EV, according to the 2025 American Community Survey released Thursday. Homeowners reported EVs at a rate of 6.4%, compared with 3.6% of renters. California led the nation at 13.8% overall, more than twice the national rate. North Dakota (1.3%), Wyoming (1.6%) and Louisiana (1.6%) ranked among the lowest. State of play: For the first time, the Census Bureau asked households with vehicles kept at home whether they owned or leased an EV, offering a nationwide snapshot of who has gone electric. A brief history of the NYC Marathon One hundred and twenty-seven runners began the first New York City Marathon on September 13, 1970. Fifty-five finished the race located in Manhattan’s Central Park, which was put on by the New York Road Runners (NYRR). It cost just a dollar to enter and $1,000 to execute. Beginning in 1976, the course expanded to include all five New York City boroughs. This change was made to celebrate America’s 200th birthday and was so popular that it stuck. The race continued even in times of adversity, showing the strength and resilience of the city. For instance, runners gave their all just two months after the September 11 attacks in 2001. During the Covid-19 pandemic, the marathon went virtual. In 2024, it became the largest marathon in history with 55,646 finishers, according to NYRR.
